title: Financial Independence
description: The savings rate, the 4% sketch, and the number 25 times spending.
wolfLine: Spending writes the target. The savings rate is the lever.

savings-rate.definition: The share of your pay that you keep instead of spending. Pay of $60,000 and savings of $15,000 is a 25% savings rate.

four-percent-rule.definition: A rule of thumb: in the first retired year, withdraw about 4% of the portfolio, then adjust that dollar amount for inflation. It is a sketch from history, not a promise.

fi-number.definition: The portfolio that could cover your yearly spending under the 4% rule of thumb. It is about 25 times yearly spending.
fi-number.example: Spending $40,000 a year points at a FI number of $1,000,000.

coast-fi.definition: Having enough invested that, with no more contributions, an example growth rate could reach your FI number by a chosen age. The rate is a guess, not a promise.
coast-fi.example: About $100,000 left alone, doubling three times, is about $800,000.

lessons.title: The Savings Rate
lessons.summary: The lever you can actually pull.

steps.title: Share of pay
steps.body: The [[savings rate]] is the share of pay you do not spend. A raise helps. A lower spending number helps more, because the rate is savings divided by pay. Investment returns are a guess. The rate is a choice.

steps.prompt: Pay is $60,000 and you save $15,000. What is the savings rate, in percent?
A $4,000 month with $1,000 saved is what percent?
steps.explain: $1,000 ÷ $4,000 = 25%. Same rate, one month.

steps.prompt: A higher savings rate requires a higher salary.
steps.explain: The rate is a share. Spending less raises it even when pay stays put.

steps.prompt: Pay stays $60,000 and you save $6,000 instead of $15,000. What is the savings rate, in percent?

steps.title: What the rule actually says
steps.body: The [[4% rule|four-percent-rule]] says: in year one of retirement, withdraw about 4% of the portfolio, then adjust that dollar amount for [[inflation]] each year. It is a rule of thumb from US history. A very long retirement, a crash in the first years, or fierce inflation can break it. It is not a guarantee, and it is not “spend 4% of whatever is left each year.”

steps.prompt: What is 4% of a $1,000,000 portfolio, in dollars, for year one?
Inflation in the example is 3%. What is the year-two withdrawal if you adjust the $40,000?
steps.explain: $40,000 × 1.03 = $41,200. You adjust the dollars, you do not take 4% of a smaller pile.

steps.prompt: The 4% rule promises the money will last no matter what the first years do.
steps.explain: Bad early returns and a very long retirement are the cracks. The rule is a sketch.

steps.prompt: Which version matches the rule?
choices: Always spend 4% of this year’s balance
Spend about 4% in year one, then adjust those dollars for inflation
Spend the whole gain, every year
steps.explain: Year one is the 4%. Later years inflate that dollar amount. They do not restart the percent on a shrunken pile.

steps.title: Turn the rule around
steps.body: If year one is 4% of the pile, the pile is 25 times spending. That portfolio is your [[FI number]]. Spending of $40,000 points at $1,000,000. Spend less, and the number shrinks. The market still has to cooperate. The number is a target, not a balance you have.

doc.title: A FI sketch
doc.subtitle: The 4% rule turned around
doc.note: 25 times spending is 1 ÷ 0.04. It is a rule of thumb, not a quote.

steps.prompt: Yearly spending is $40,000. What is 25 times that, in dollars?
Spending is $30,000 a year. What is the FI number?
steps.explain: 25 × $30,000 = $750,000. A lower life has a lower target.

steps.prompt: The FI number is the salary you need to earn forever.
steps.explain: It is a portfolio target, about 25 times spending. Pay is how you feed it. Spending is what sets it.

steps.prompt: How many dollars of yearly spending does a $500,000 FI number describe, at 4%?

steps.title: Two targets, one person
steps.body: Regular FI uses the spending you actually want. Lean FI uses a smaller life on purpose. Neither is more virtuous. A lean [[FI number]] is just a smaller multiple. If regular spending is $40,000, the target is $1,000,000. Lean spending of $25,000 is $625,000.

steps.prompt: What is the lean FI number on $25,000 of yearly spending?
How many fewer dollars is that than the $1,000,000 regular target?
steps.explain: $1,000,000 − $625,000 = $375,000. The gap is the spending you agreed to skip.

steps.prompt: Lean FI means the 4% rule no longer has cracks.
steps.explain: A smaller pile can still be hit by a bad early retirement. Lean changes the target, not the uncertainty.

steps.prompt: What actually changed between the two numbers?
choices: How much life you are asking the portfolio to buy
steps.explain: Spending sets the number. Lean is a smaller ask.

lessons.title: Coast FI
lessons.summary: Enough that the example could finish the job.

steps.title: Stop adding, on paper
steps.body: [[Coast FI]] means the pile you already have could reach the [[FI number]] by a chosen age if you never add another dollar. This sketch uses an example 8% rate. The [[rule of 72]] says that doubles in about 9 years. Three doubles is 27 years, and 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. So $100,000 might become about $800,000. The 8% is an example, not a promise.

steps.prompt: At an example 8%, about how many years does the rule of 72 give for one doubling?
steps.explain: 72 ÷ 8 = 9 years. About, and only at that example rate.

steps.prompt: $100,000 doubles three times. About how many dollars is that?
steps.explain: $100,000 × 2 × 2 × 2 = $800,000. Three example doubles, no new deposits.

steps.prompt: Coast FI means you can stop saving and the result is guaranteed.
steps.explain: The doubling is an example rate. A lower rate, or spending that creeps up, moves the finish line.

steps.prompt: What are you allowed to stop, in the coast idea?
steps.explain: Contributions. The life, the cash pile, and the guess about returns are still there.

lessons.title: An Ordinary Income
lessons.summary: The number follows spending, not a job title.

steps.title: A teacher-sized life
steps.body: Financial independence is not a fortune reserved for a huge salary. A household that can live on $30,000 a year is aiming at about $750,000 under the [[4% rule|four-percent-rule]]. A household that spends $80,000 is aiming at $2,000,000. The salary helps you save. The spending writes the target.

steps.prompt: What is the FI number for $30,000 of yearly spending?
What is the FI number for $80,000 of yearly spending?
A modest salary makes a FI number impossible.
steps.explain: The number is 25 times spending. A modest life is a smaller number, and the savings rate is the lever.

steps.prompt: Which change shrinks the FI number?
steps.explain: Lower spending, smaller multiple. The headline does not rewrite the formula.

steps.title: The gap is the rate
steps.body: Both pages start from $60,000 of pay. One saves 10%, which is $6,000. The other saves 25%, which is $15,000. Returns are not on the page. The only difference is the [[savings rate]].

steps.prompt: Which page puts more dollars to work this year?
steps.explain: 25% is $15,000. 10% is $6,000. Same pay, $9,000 more saved on the higher rate.

steps.prompt: How many more dollars does the 25% page save this year?
The 10% page will catch up automatically, because returns are required to be higher for people who save less.
steps.explain: Nothing promises a higher return for a lower rate. The deposit gap is real every year.

steps.prompt: Over 10 years, before any growth, how many more dollars does the 25% path deposit?
steps.explain: 10 × $9,000 = $90,000. Growth, if it comes, is on top of a larger pile.

lessons.title: Dana’s 15-Year Plan
lessons.summary: The target is a million. The deposits are not.

story.title: Fifteen years, written down
story.body:
Dana can live on **$40,000** a year, so her FI number is **$1,000,000**. She saves **$15,000** a year.

Fifteen years of deposits, before growth, are **$225,000**. She writes down the gap so the plan stays honest.

steps.title: Meet Dana
steps.body:
Dana is 32 and a nurse. She can live on $40,000 a year, so her [[FI number]] under the 4% rule is $1,000,000. She saves $15,000 a year, a 25% rate on $60,000 of pay.

Fifteen years of those deposits, before any growth, are $225,000. The rest of the million would have to come from growth. She writes that down so the plan does not pretend the deposits alone finish the job.

steps.prompt: What is Dana’s FI number?
How many dollars does she deposit in 15 years, before growth?
How many dollars of the $1,000,000 are not covered by those deposits alone?
steps.explain: $1,000,000 − $225,000 = $775,000. That gap is what growth would have to cover, and growth is not a promise.

steps.prompt: Dana is guaranteed to reach $1,000,000 in 15 years because she has a plan.
steps.explain: The deposits are $225,000. The rest depends on returns and on her spending staying near $40,000.

lessons.title: Sharpen Up
lessons.summary: Smart repetition on what you’re closest to forgetting.

lessons.title: Den Trial: Financial Independence
lessons.summary: 8 questions. Three strikes and you’re out.

steps.prompt: You save $12,000 of $48,000 pay. What is the savings rate, in percent?
Spending is $50,000 a year. What is the FI number under the 25-times sketch?
The 4% rule means you spend 4% of whatever balance is left, every year.
steps.explain: Year one is about 4%. Later years adjust those dollars for inflation. They do not restart the percent.

steps.prompt: $50,000 doubles three times at an example rate. About how many dollars is that?
steps.explain: $50,000 × 2 × 2 × 2 = $400,000. The rate that produced the doubles is still an example.
